source.title: AdaVid: Adaptive Video-Language Pretraining
source.authors: Chaitanya Patel; Juan Carlos Niebles; Ehsan Adeli

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent cutoff or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Evaluates downstream performance at different adaptive compute settings in video-language models, extending scale-related evaluation to a video setting; it does not fit or test the original held-out-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream benchmark performance across adaptive embedding-dimension and compute configurations, which bears on V6. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, fit power laws, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Comparisons of other benchmark baselines without a varying scale condition are not rows for V6.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It trains one adaptive video encoder and slices its embedding width at inference to trade accuracy for FLOPs. It does not train models at different parameter counts, token counts or training compute, and fits no scaling relation. Hoffmann et al. is cited only to count attention FLOPs (Appendix A.1). Accuracy versus inference-time sub-network width inside one trained model is a related but different construct from V6's downstream gains with scale or pretraining loss, so it goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that AdaVid gives one adaptive video encoder that matches or beats EgoVLP and HierVL at full width and keeps strong performance at reduced inference compute.
record.recipe_differences: Uses adaptive transformer embedding dimensions and evaluates downstream accuracy and compute; it does not fit held-out-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer-wise dimension ordering affects performance: training with gradually decreasing dimensions performs better than training with increasing dimensions. The text also reports a small accuracy drop at the lowest-compute configuration, especially on EgoMCQ (intra).

fits_no_version.finding: In one adaptive-width video encoder, zero-shot accuracy rises with inference FLOPs set by embedding width. EgoSchema subset reads 52.0 / 54.2 / 56.2 at 20 / 75 / 293 FLOPs×10^10, with small drops on EgoMCQ and SummaryMCQ down to 0.25x. Configurations that decrease width with depth beat those that increase it at equal FLOPs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a nested (Matryoshka-style) model, downstream accuracy rises monotonically and saturates with inference-time width or compute.

fits_no_version.finding: More input frames at reduced width raise Diving-48 accuracy within a given compute: 81.0 at 64 frames versus 82.2 at 128 frames.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For video encoders, trading width for frame count improves the accuracy–compute trade-off on temporal tasks.

record.peer_reviewed: 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are stated. Several scale-varying results are described qualitatively or appear only in figures, without exact values in the text. The study evaluates adaptive compute settings within its video models rather than fitting or validating predictive scaling laws.
record.rows_left_out: Left out standalone benchmark comparisons that do not vary scale or compute, including full-capacity EgoMCQ baseline comparisons in Table 2 and full-capacity SummaryMCQ comparisons in Table 4. Figure 3, Figure 5, and Figure 6 numerical values not stated in the text are recorded qualitatively where the text describes their trends.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fits in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
No allocation between parameters and tokens at fixed compute.
Layer-wise width configurations of one trained model are compared, but not separately trained models of different shape at a fixed parameter count.
Video models are used, but no power-law form is tested.
No downstream performance across model or training scale, and none related to pretraining loss.
No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with a V6 limits_scope verdict is wrong. The compute variation is inference-time slicing of a single trained model, not scaling of model or training. Hoffmann et al. is cited only for the FLOPs formula. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run losses are reported.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and training tokens is evaluated.
The study varies layer embedding dimensions, not depth and width at a fixed parameter count to measure architecture sensitivity.
The study concerns video-language models, but does not test whether a power-law form holds for video or other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

Tests downstream video benchmark performance across adaptive compute settings; does not fit a predictive scaling relation, evaluate language-model downstream tasks, or relate performance to pretraining loss.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted or compared across setup and fitting choices.
